Reproductive ecology of Common ponyfish, Leiognathus equula, has been examined in several coastal populations across its Indo-Pacific range. Field surveys in the Gulf of Thailand demonstrated that spawning occurs primarily during the warmer monsoon months, when surface temperatures reach 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, the incubation period from fertilisation to eclosion is remarkably brief, with hatching occurring just 2.7 days [ab = 2.7 days] after gamete release at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This accelerated embryonic development is consistent with the rapid life histories observed in many small-bodied leiognathids. Newly emerged prolarvae possess a modest yolk reserve, and the initial mass of these lecithotrophic offspring, corresponding to a newly hatched wet weight at birth of 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], reflects the small egg diameter of approximately 0.8 mm. This minimal starting mass imposes a tight energetic constraint during the transition to exogenous feeding.

As larvae develop, they undergo a pelagic phase lasting several weeks before initiating metamorphosis. Growth trajectories derived from otolith increment analysis indicate that individuals reach a total length at puberty of 10.7 cm [Lp = 10.7 cm], a milestone that typically coincides with the completion of juvenile morphological transformation and the onset of gonadal maturation. This length is substantially smaller than the maximum ultimate total length of 28 cm [Li = 28 cm] recorded in the species, illustrating the extended period of somatic growth that continues well after sexual maturation. The length-weight relationship for the species, based on extensive sampling across multiple habitats, allows estimation of asymptotic body mass. From this relationship, the corresponding ultimate wet weight of a 28 cm individual is calculated to be approximately 445 grams [Wwi = approximately 445 grams], a value that represents the upper bound of mass for this relatively small ponyfish.

Longevity estimates for Leiognathus equula are derived from length-frequency data and validated by marginal increment analysis of sagittal otoliths. At the typical ambient temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C] prevailing in their tropical habitat, the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years]. This lifespan, while modest compared to larger teleosts, is not unusual for a fish of this body size and reflects a life history strategy characterised by early maturation and high natural mortality. Interestingly, captive-reared individuals maintained at this same temperature regime have been observed to reach comparable ages, suggesting that the species' intrinsic longevity is relatively fixed under optimal thermal conditions. The consistency between field and laboratory estimates strengthens confidence in the 5 year maximum longevity figure.

Comparative studies within the Leiognathidae reveal considerable interspecific variation in growth parameters and body size. The ultimate total length recorded for Common ponyfish, 28 cm [Li = 28 cm], places it among the medium-sized members of the genus, with some congeneric species achieving substantially larger maximum sizes. The length at which 50% of females attain maturity, documented at 10.7 cm [Lp = 10.7 cm], appears to be a conservative estimate reflecting the onset of vitellogenesis in this subtropical population. Seasonal variability in food availability may modulate the precise timing of maturation, but the 10.7 cm threshold remains a robust indicator across years. The total wet weight of a mature female approaching this pubertal length is considerably less than the asymptotic mass of 445 grams [Wwi = 445 grams], underscoring the substantial investment in somatic tissue required to reach full adult size.

Physiological studies of larval energetics have further refined our understanding of early life constraints in Leiognathus equula. The mass of newly hatched yolk-sac larvae, 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], represents an extremely small starting capital that necessitates rapid onset of exogenous feeding to avoid starvation. At the standard rearing temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the window between hatching and the point of no return is narrow, with first feeding typically commencing within 2.7 days [ab = 2.7 days]. In contrast, the species exhibits a relatively extended adult phase, with the maximum lifespan of 5 years [am = 5 years] at this temperature allowing for multiple spawning seasons over an individual's lifetime at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This iteroparous strategy, combined with high fecundity, likely buffers populations against sporadic recruitment failures in variable coastal environments.
